QF.id: AIFM AIFs in India and Suitability_5

question.text: Ms. Meera Subramanian, aged 42, has an INR 100 crore portfolio currently invested 25% Large-cap, 25% Small-cap, 20% Unlisted, 15% Listed Corporate Debt, 10% G-Secs, 5% Money Market. She has capped her exposure to any single asset class at 40%. She wishes to re-allocate the 20% Unlisted allocation (INR 20 crore) into Category III AIFs, choosing between Fund A (long-short, Mid-cap only) and Fund B (market-neutral, 80% Small-cap and 20% Mid-cap). As her fund manager, which re-allocation is MOST consistent with her concentration policy?

answer.text: Allocate the entire INR 20 crore to Fund B for diversification benefits
Split INR 10 crore each to Fund A and Fund B
Allocate the entire INR 20 crore to Fund A
Retain the allocation in domestic unlisted securities since any Cat III allocation will breach her cap

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Her existing Small-cap exposure is already 25%. Fund B would inject 80% of INR 20 crore = INR 16 crore (16% of portfolio) additional Small-cap, taking Small-cap to 25% + 16% = 41% — breaching the 40% cap. Fund A (Mid-cap) does not touch Small-cap, and the chapter's own Example 3 concludes that the full INR 20 crore should go to Fund A in this scenario. **The Trap:** Option A looks diversified but mechanically breaches the 40% Small-cap cap. Option B is a false compromise — still adds ~8% Small-cap on top of existing 25%, which is tolerable but inferior to a compliant full allocation. Option D ignores that the investor already decided to re-allocate. **Cross-Exam Context:** X-A/B Investment Adviser exams test look-through concentration analysis; XIX-C expects the Manager to articulate how an AIF's underlying exposures feed into an LP's overall asset-class caps — a crucial conversation in IC meetings with family offices. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** For family-office LPs with hard concentration caps, request a look-through statement every quarter and model the Cat III fund's current exposures into the LP's master portfolio — don't wait for the annual report, concentration breaches attract regulatory scrutiny from the LP's own auditor.
